title: Ten questions about the Labour Codes, answered briefly
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Ten common questions on the Labour Codes, from floor wage and gratuity to gig work, strikes and night shifts, answered in plain language.
body:
Since the four Labour Codes came into force, workers and karyakartas have been asking the same practical questions again and again. What has changed for me? What can I claim? Where do I complain? This post answers ten of the most common ones in plain language, drawing on the Labour Ministry's own summaries and FAQs and on reports of the rules notified so far. Please note one general warning at the outset: the law is new, the rules are still being completed, and the position in your State may differ from the Central position described here.

## The basics: what is in force

**1. Which Codes are in force?** The Government announced that the four Codes (Wages, Industrial Relations, Social Security, and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions) took effect on 21 November 2025, consolidating 29 earlier Central labour laws ([Business Standard](https://www.business-standard.com/india-news/labour-codes-labour-laws-ministry-of-labour-central-govt-125112100754_1.html)). The Centre notified its final rules on 8 and 9 May 2026. Those rules apply directly only where the Central Government is the "appropriate Government", such as railways, mines, banking and insurance. Other employers follow their State's rules, and many States are still finalising them ([Bar & Bench](https://www.barandbench.com/view-point/the-next-phase-of-workforce-compliance-what-the-newly-notified-central-labour-rules-mean-for-employers)). In the meantime, the Ministry has said that existing rules continue where they are consistent with the Codes ([SCC Online on the Ministry's FAQs](https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2026/01/03/labour-ministry-issued-faqs-on-the-labour-codes/)).

## Wages and pay

**2. Does the minimum wage now apply to everyone?** According to the Ministry's FAQs, the Wages Code covers all employees, including full-time, part-time, temporary, casual and contract workers. Minimum wages are fixed by the Central and State Governments within their areas, after consulting workers' and employers' representatives, and flexible working hours cannot be used to reduce the minimum wage ([SCC Online](https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2026/01/03/labour-ministry-issued-faqs-on-the-labour-codes/)). The older approach, in which minimum wages applied only to listed "scheduled" employments, has been replaced.

**3. What is a floor wage?** It is a national baseline set by the Central Government. Minimum wages fixed by the Centre or a State must be above it, and a State minimum wage that is already higher cannot be reduced ([PRS Legislative Research](https://prsindia.org/billtrack/prs-products/prs-bill-summary-3305)). A report from July 2026 said that the Government had not announced a date for notifying the National Floor Wage, that it was setting up a 15-member Central Advisory Board for consultation, and that the earlier, non-statutory floor level was Rs 176 per day, last revised in 2017 ([Angel One](https://www.angelone.in/news/economy/government-initiates-national-floor-wage-exercise-with-advisory-board)). So, at the time of writing, a statutory floor wage figure is still awaited.

**4. What if my wages are delayed or wrongly cut?** The Code caps total deductions at 50 per cent of wages, and the Central rules require an employer to give an employee seven days to explain before deducting for damage or loss ([PRS](https://prsindia.org/billtrack/prs-products/prs-bill-summary-3305); [Bar & Bench](https://www.barandbench.com/view-point/the-next-phase-of-workforce-compliance-what-the-newly-notified-central-labour-rules-mean-for-employers)). The Labour Ministry's summary also says that wages must be paid on time and that unauthorised deductions are prohibited, with some sector-specific timelines, such as salary by the 7th of the month in IT and ITES ([Labour Ministry release](https://labour.gov.in/sites/default/files/pib2192463.pdf)). Complaints go to the inspector-cum-facilitator or the authority under the Code. The inspector-cum-facilitator is meant to guide employers towards compliance as well as to enforce the law, so a written complaint, with a copy to your union, is the right first step. Keep your wage slips and bank statements.

## Gratuity and fixed-term work

**5. Who gets gratuity?** Gratuity is payable on termination, superannuation, resignation, death or disablement, or expiry of a fixed-term contract. The standard rate is 15 days' wages for each completed year of service, with a part of a year beyond six months counted as a full year, and the current maximum is Rs 20 lakh ([SCC Online](https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2026/01/03/labour-ministry-issued-faqs-on-the-labour-codes/)). The big change is for fixed-term employees: they become eligible after one year of service, with pro rata gratuity, compared with the five years that applied before ([Labour Ministry release](https://labour.gov.in/sites/default/files/pib2192463.pdf)). The Central rules add that a further period of more than six months in a fixed-term contract is rounded up to a full year for the calculation ([Bar & Bench](https://www.barandbench.com/view-point/the-next-phase-of-workforce-compliance-what-the-newly-notified-central-labour-rules-mean-for-employers)). For other employees the general rule remains five years of continuous service.

**6. Do I get an appointment letter?** Yes. The Government's summary says that appointment letters are mandatory for all workers, stating designation, wages and social security entitlements, and the Central rules prescribe a format that includes the establishment's labour identification number and the employee's Universal Account Number. Fixed-term employees are meant to receive the same core benefits as permanent staff, including provident fund, ESI and minimum wages.

## Gig, platform and contract workers

**7. Are gig workers covered?** The Social Security Code defines gig work, platform work and aggregators for the first time. Aggregators are to contribute between 1 and 2 per cent of annual turnover, capped at 5 per cent of what they pay to gig and platform workers, and workers get an Aadhaar-linked Universal Account Number so that benefits can move with them across States ([Business Standard](https://www.business-standard.com/india-news/labour-codes-labour-laws-ministry-of-labour-central-govt-125112100754_1.html)). In June 2026 the Labour Ministry directed online aggregators to complete their linkage with the e-Shram portal by 21 June, and reported that 15 major aggregators, among them Zomato, Swiggy, Uber and Ola, had already joined ([SCC Online](https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2026/06/02/eshram-deadline-aggregators-june-21-gig-workers/)). If you work through an app, check that you are registered on e-Shram.

**8. What about contract workers?** The licensing threshold for contract labour has been raised from 20 to 50 workers, which the Ministry says is for administrative ease and does not reduce protections. The Code does not distinguish between regular, contract and inter-State migrant workers in extending benefits ([SCC Online](https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2026/01/03/labour-ministry-issued-faqs-on-the-labour-codes/)). Under the Central rules, principal employers bear primary welfare responsibility and are liable for a contractor's unpaid wages and bonus, and a grievance committee must resolve a contract worker's complaint within 30 days, failing which it goes electronically to the inspector-cum-facilitator ([Mondaq](https://www.mondaq.com/india/employee-rights-labour-relations/1807196/cracking-the-code-ii-the-new-central-labour-rules-at-a-glance)). Contract workers should ask their principal employer, in writing, for the name of the contractor and the licence number.

## Strikes, disputes and women's work

**9. Can I strike?** The Industrial Relations Code does not ban strikes; the right remains, subject to notice. Summaries of the Code describe a requirement of advance notice, with a strike not to take place within 14 days of giving the notice and before the date specified in the notice has arrived ([Lawrbit summary](https://www.lawrbit.com/?p=2563)). The Ministry's FAQ speaks of 14 days' notice. Because notice periods and the sectors they cover matter a great deal, a union should read the Code's strike provisions and the applicable rules, or take advice, before any notice is served. Disputes go to a two-member industrial tribunal system, with direct access after conciliation ([Labour Ministry release](https://labour.gov.in/sites/default/files/pib2192463.pdf)).

**10. Can women work at night?** Yes, with safeguards. The Ministry's FAQ says that women may work in any establishment, including night shifts, but only with their consent, and employers must provide adequate safety and transport arrangements. The Central rules add that for work before 6 a.m. or after 7 p.m., consent, transport and displayed emergency numbers are required ([Bar & Bench](https://www.barandbench.com/view-point/the-next-phase-of-workforce-compliance-what-the-newly-notified-central-labour-rules-mean-for-employers)).

## Where to read the law and what BMS has said

The authoritative text of the Codes and the rules is on India Code and on the Ministry of Labour and Employment's website. Always read the original, since reports and explainers, including this one, can be incomplete. BMS has welcomed all four Codes while stating that it has concerns about provisions in the Industrial Relations Code and the OSH Code, and it has called the Wages and Social Security Codes historic ([BMS statement, 31 January 2026](https://www.bms.org.in/?p=9332)).

*This is a general guide, not legal advice. Please consult the text of the Codes and rules for your State and, if needed, an advocate.*
